questions.q: Virus free plants are developed from :
questions.solution:
The apical meristem (shoot tip) of an infected plant is usually **free of virus**: it has no vascular tissue for the virus to travel in, and its cells divide faster than the virus multiplies.

Culturing this meristem therefore yields **virus-free plants**, as done for banana, potato and sugarcane.

questions.q: Who is regarded as the father of plant tissue culture?
questions.solution:
**Gottlieb Haberlandt** (1902) first tried to culture isolated plant cells and put forward the idea of totipotency.

Steward later raised whole carrot plants from single cells, and Murashige and Skoog devised the MS medium (1962).

questions.q: The ability of a single plant cell to develop into a complete plant is called:
questions.solution:
**Totipotency** is the inherent capacity of a living plant cell to give rise to a whole plant, because each cell carries the full genetic information.

It is the basic principle on which plant tissue culture rests.

questions.q: The most widely used nutrient medium in plant tissue culture is:
questions.solution:
**MS medium**, devised by Murashige and Skoog (1962), supplies macro- and micronutrients, vitamins, sucrose as the carbon source and growth regulators. It is the most widely used plant tissue culture medium.

Nutrient agar and Czapek medium are for microbes; Hoagland solution is for hydroponics.

Media are sterilised in an **autoclave** at 121 °C and 15 lbs/sq inch pressure for 15–20 minutes.

Mercuric chloride and ethanol are used for explants (surface sterilisation), and flaming for instruments.

questions.q: A high cytokinin to auxin ratio in the medium promotes the formation of:
questions.solution:
Skoog and Miller showed that organ formation depends on the balance of hormones: a **high cytokinin : auxin** ratio favours **shoots**, a high auxin : cytokinin ratio favours roots, and a balance keeps the callus growing.

This is used to regenerate whole plants from callus.

questions.q: The gelling agent commonly added to make a solid culture medium is:
questions.solution:
**Agar**, a polysaccharide from red algae, solidifies the medium (about 0.8%). It is not digested by plant tissues and stays firm at culture temperatures.

Sucrose is the carbon source, not a gelling agent.

questions.q: The chemical commonly used as a fusogen in protoplast fusion is:
questions.solution:
Protoplasts are released by digesting cell walls with **cellulase and pectinase**, then fused with **polyethylene glycol (PEG)** or an electric pulse (electrofusion) to give somatic hybrids such as Pomato.

Colchicine doubles chromosomes; it does not fuse cells.

questions.q: Somatic embryos are encapsulated to make artificial seeds using:
questions.solution:
**Artificial (synthetic) seeds** are somatic embryos coated in a gel of **sodium alginate**, which hardens into beads when dropped into calcium chloride solution.

The bead protects the embryo and supplies nutrients, so it can be stored, transported and sown like a seed.

questions.q: At what temperature, in °C, is a culture medium autoclaved?
questions.solution:
Media are autoclaved at **121 °C** under 15 lbs/sq inch pressure for 15–20 minutes.

At this pressure steam reaches 121 °C, high enough to kill bacterial and fungal spores.

questions.q: At what temperature, in °C, is plant material stored in liquid nitrogen during cryopreservation?
questions.solution:
Cryopreservation stores cells, embryos or meristems in **liquid nitrogen at −196 °C**, where metabolism virtually stops.

Cryoprotectants such as DMSO or glycerol are added first to prevent damage from ice crystals.

questions.q: To what pH is a plant tissue culture medium usually adjusted before autoclaving?
questions.solution:
The pH of the medium is adjusted to about **5.8** (the usual range is 5.6–5.8), slightly acidic, using dilute NaOH or HCl.

At this pH nutrients stay available and the agar sets properly.

questions.q: What is the undifferentiated, unorganised mass of cells formed from an explant on a medium with auxin called?
questions.solution:
The explant's cells dedifferentiate and divide repeatedly, forming an unorganised mass called **callus**.

Callus can be subcultured, used for suspension cultures, or made to redifferentiate into shoots, roots or somatic embryos.

questions.q: What pressure, in lbs per square inch, is used when autoclaving culture media?
questions.solution:
Autoclaving is done at **15 lbs/sq inch** (about 1.06 kg/cm²), which raises steam to 121 °C, for 15–20 minutes.

Heat-sensitive substances such as some vitamins and hormones are filter-sterilised instead and added afterwards.

questions.q: Describe the basic steps involved in plant tissue culture.
questions.solution:
Plant tissue culture grows plant cells, tissues or organs on a nutrient medium under aseptic, controlled conditions. It rests on **totipotency**.

**1. Preparation of the medium**: MS medium with macro- and micronutrients, vitamins, sucrose, growth regulators (auxin, cytokinin) and agar; pH adjusted to about 5.8.

**2. Sterilisation**: glassware and medium in an autoclave (121 °C, 15 lbs/sq inch, 15–20 min); explants surface-sterilised with 0.1% mercuric chloride or 70% ethanol; work done in a laminar airflow chamber.

**3. Inoculation**: the sterilised explant (shoot tip, leaf, node, embryo) is transferred aseptically onto the medium.

**4. Incubation**: cultures are kept at 25 ± 2 °C with a 16-hour light period and 50–60% relative humidity. The explant forms **callus**.

**5. Regeneration**: by changing the auxin : cytokinin ratio the callus forms shoots and roots (organogenesis) or somatic embryos (embryogenesis).

**6. Hardening**: plantlets are moved to pots in a greenhouse and gradually exposed to natural conditions before planting in the field.
